title: 3rd Stopping Place 4th Truth 2 Kinds Of Provision

questions.question: What is the second kind of provision described in the passage?
questions.answer: It is a man-made, non-essential kind of provision that grows out of habit, excess, and wrong use until it seems necessary.

questions.question: How is this second kind of provision different from the first kind in terms of guarantee?
questions.answer: It is not assured in the same way; it depends on Divine generosity and may or may not be given.

questions.question: What attitude is praised for a person dealing with this second kind of provision?
questions.answer: Living with moderation, being content, and seeking livelihood through lawful effort with the intention of worship.

questions.question: Why is frugality presented as something positive in the passage?
questions.answer: It brings peace and satisfaction, and it helps a person live gratefully instead of chasing unnecessary wants.

questions.question: What makes a person “wretched” in this section?
questions.answer: Wastefulness and greed lead the person to leave lawful effort, become morally and spiritually degraded, and live in misery.

questions.question: Besides the stomach, what other human faculties are said to need provision?
questions.answer: The inner and outer faculties such as the heart, spirit, mind, eye, ear, and mouth.

questions.question: What kind of provision do these other faculties receive?
questions.answer: Each receives a fitting kind of nourishment suited to its nature, bringing joy and benefit.

questions.question: Why are faculties like the eye, ear, imagination, and intellect compared to keys?
questions.answer: Because they open the way to different forms of mercy and allow a person to receive special blessings.

questions.question: What example is given to explain how one of these “keys” works?
questions.answer: The eye is described as opening access to the beauty and attractiveness spread across the world.

questions.question: What role does faith play in benefiting from these faculties?
questions.answer: Faith allows a person to make proper use of them and receive their deeper benefit.

questions.question: Into how many kinds is provision divided in this passage, and which one is discussed here?
questions.answer: It is divided into two kinds, and this section explains the second kind.

questions.question: What causes the second kind of provision to appear necessary even though it is not truly necessary?
questions.answer: Repeated habits, extravagance, and misuse make it feel like a real need.

questions.question: What does the passage teach about whether this second kind of provision always comes?
questions.answer: It teaches that it is not always given; it depends on Divine generosity.

questions.question: How should a believer view modest living and lawful work in relation to worship?
questions.answer: They should see them as part of worship and as a practical form of asking Allah for provision.

questions.question: What emotional and spiritual state belongs to the person praised in this section?
questions.answer: That person lives with gratitude, appreciation, happiness, and inward peace.

questions.question: What chain of harm begins with extravagance and greed?
questions.answer: It leads to leaving lawful effort, humiliating dependence, laziness, wrongdoing, and a miserable life.

questions.question: What comparison is made between bodily hunger and the needs of the inner human being?
questions.answer: Just as the body needs food, the inner faculties and senses also need their own nourishment.

questions.question: Name three non-physical human faculties mentioned as receiving provision.
questions.answer: The heart, the spirit, and the intellect.

questions.question: What does it mean that each faculty receives provision “in appropriate form”?
questions.answer: Each one is given the kind of nourishment that matches its own function and nature.

questions.question: Why were human faculties created as openings to mercy?
questions.answer: So people could receive richer blessings and take delight in the many gifts placed in creation.

questions.question: What is meant by “metaphorical and artificial” provision in this passage?
questions.answer: It means forms of consumption that are not basic to life but are treated as if they were necessary because of unhealthy patterns.

questions.question: According to the passage, what are the roots of this artificial kind of provision?
questions.answer: It comes from dependence on habits, overuse, and wasteful living.

questions.question: What does the passage imply about expecting this second kind of provision as a right?
questions.answer: A person should not treat it as guaranteed or owed to him.

questions.question: Which qualities are joined together in the description of the fortunate person?
questions.answer: Frugality, contentment, lawful striving, gratitude, and appreciation.

questions.question: Why is lawful striving linked with prayer in this section?
questions.answer: Because honest effort is presented as a practical way of turning to Allah for sustenance.

questions.question: What moral warning is given about greed?
questions.answer: Greed does not enrich a person spiritually; it pushes him into disgrace and hardship.

questions.question: What broader meaning of “provision” appears in the second half of the passage?
questions.answer: Provision includes not only food for the body but also nourishment for the senses and inner faculties.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the source of this wider provision?
questions.answer: It comes from the mercy of the Compassionate Provider.

questions.question: What effect does this provision have on the human faculties?
questions.answer: It delights them, benefits them, and fulfills their particular needs.

questions.question: How is the eye used to illustrate the idea of inner provision?
questions.answer: It is shown as receiving joy and nourishment through perceiving the beauty spread throughout creation.

questions.question: What false impression can develop about the second form of provision?
questions.answer: People can begin to think something optional is actually necessary.

questions.question: What does the passage say determines whether this second form is given?
questions.answer: It is given according to Divine generosity, not as a fixed guarantee.

questions.question: Why is the person called “happy” in this section?
questions.answer: Because he lives simply, works lawfully, stays content, and receives what comes with thankfulness.

questions.question: How does the passage connect happiness with frugality?
questions.answer: It presents moderation as a source of ease and pleasure rather than deprivation.

questions.question: What actions show that someone has fallen into greed and excess?
questions.answer: He abandons proper effort, seeks gain from every possible source, becomes lazy, and acts wrongly.

questions.question: What does the passage teach about the human person by mentioning the heart, spirit, and intellect?
questions.answer: It teaches that the human being has deeper dimensions that need nourishment beyond physical food.

questions.question: Why is it important that each faculty receives provision separately?
questions.answer: Because each faculty has a different role and therefore needs its own fitting kind of nourishment.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the purpose of the senses and inner powers?
questions.answer: They were made to receive and enjoy signs of Divine mercy.

questions.question: How does the example of the eye deepen the idea of provision?
questions.answer: It shows that seeing beauty is also a kind of sustenance, not just eating and drinking.

questions.question: What is the meaning of saying these faculties benefit “through faith”?
questions.answer: Faith allows a person to understand these gifts correctly and use them in a way that brings real gain.

questions.question: What practical problem does the second kind of provision begin with?
questions.answer: People become attached to unnecessary things until they treat them like basic needs.

questions.question: How does the passage describe Allah’s relation to this unnecessary type of provision?
questions.answer: It says Allah may give it out of generosity, but it is not promised in the same way as essential sustenance.

questions.question: What three qualities define the fortunate person in dealing with provision?
questions.answer: Simplicity, contentment, and lawful effort.

questions.question: In what way is grateful living connected to worship in the passage?
questions.answer: Receiving blessings thankfully and seeking livelihood in a lawful way are treated as acts of devotion.

questions.question: What inner condition stands behind the “wretched” life described here?
questions.answer: A restless craving driven by greed and wastefulness.

questions.question: What are two results of greed mentioned in the passage?
questions.answer: It leads to humiliation in seeking from others and to a miserable, morally damaged life.

questions.question: Why does the passage move from the stomach to the heart and mind?
questions.answer: To show that human need is not only physical but also emotional, spiritual, and intellectual.

questions.question: What does it mean that the faculties “request” their sustenance?
questions.answer: Each faculty has its own natural longing for what completes and pleases it.

questions.question: From where is this non-physical provision said to come?
questions.answer: It comes from the treasury of mercy.

questions.question: What is the function of calling the faculties “keys”?
questions.answer: It shows that they are means by which a person reaches and receives different Divine gifts.

questions.question: What can the eye receive as its share of provision?
questions.answer: It receives joy through witnessing the beauty and loveliness placed in the world.

questions.question: How does the passage define the second form of sustenance in relation to habit?
questions.answer: It is shaped by habits that turn nonessential things into seeming necessities.

questions.question: What does this section teach about human expectations regarding extra comforts?
questions.answer: People should not assume such comforts are guaranteed.

questions.question: What way of life is presented as blessed and healthy?
questions.answer: A life of moderation, contentment, lawful work, and thankful acceptance of what one receives.

questions.question: Why is lawful striving honored in this passage?
questions.answer: Because it is a proper and worshipful way of seeking provision.

questions.question: How is extravagance evaluated here?
questions.answer: It is treated as a cause of misery and loss.

questions.question: What kind of character is formed by greed according to the passage?
questions.answer: It forms a person who is dependent, idle, unjust, and unhappy.

questions.question: What important idea is taught by saying the heart, spirit, eye, and ear also need sustenance?
questions.answer: Human beings are made for many levels of nourishment, not just physical survival.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the Provider’s care for these different faculties?
questions.answer: Each one is given fitting gifts that gladden it and meet its particular need.

questions.question: Why might the creation of these faculties as “keys” be considered an act of generosity?
questions.answer: Because it allows human beings to access many forms of mercy in rich and varied ways.

questions.question: What is one example of a treasury opened by a human faculty?
questions.answer: The eye opens onto the beauty present throughout the universe.

questions.question: What conclusion can be drawn from the statement that all the faculties benefit through faith?
questions.answer: Faith is what turns these capacities into true means of receiving mercy and joy.
